title: Reconciling, when safe
hookLine: where it's safe, reconciliation is a gift to both

cards: Two old friends pass in a grocery aisle. One hand goes halfway up, the other person nods, and both keep walking, carts rattling, each wondering if the other wanted to stop.
A few weeks ago this path said forgiving doesn't require going back to the relationship, and that's still true. But sometimes the distance isn't protecting anyone anymore.
Sometimes the other person is safe, and sorry, or just as stuck. A Hebrew psalm and a Chinese classic each have a line about what happens when two people do stop.

teach.b: First, what it's for. Psalm 133 opens, in the King James words: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Not only right, but sweet to live in.
The psalm compares it to fragrant oil running down Aaron's beard, and to dew falling on the mountains: things that run down and spread, reaching whatever they touch. Second, the honest catch.
The Tao Te Ching, in chapter seventy-nine, says, in a paraphrase of James Legge's version, that when a great quarrel is settled, some resentment is sure to remain. Reconciling isn't a time machine.
Two people who make up still remember. Third, what the wise one does with that.
The same chapter pictures a tally, the old way of recording a debt in two halves, and says the sage keeps his half and doesn't press the other side to pay.
One way to read it: reconciling isn't pretending there was no debt. It's holding the record without collecting on it. Fourth, the condition in your line.
Reconciling is only a gift where it's safe. If the other person is still dangerous, still cruel, still doing the thing, the brave act may be the boundary from a few days ago, not the reunion.
Nothing on this path asks anyone to walk back into harm.
But where it is safe, a half-raised hand in a grocery aisle can be the start of something good and pleasant.

how: Jews and Christians pray Psalm 133, and its opening Hebrew words, hinneh mah tov, are sung as a song in many Jewish communities; readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter 79 as counsel on not pressing old claims after a quarrel.

o: pretending the old quarrel never happened at all
forgiving someone privately without ever seeing them
two people rebuilding what broke, only where it's safe

games.q: two lines on making up — tap the pairs.

s: Psalm 133 calls brothers living together in unity good and pleasant
"behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!"
Tao Te Ching 79 says that once a great quarrel is settled, no resentment remains
it says some resentment is sure to remain, and pictures the sage not pressing for payment.
on this path, reconciling is asked of everyone, safe or not
only where it's safe; where harm continues, the boundary comes first.

games.q: you and an old friend have made up, but a little resentment still lingers. what does Tao Te Ching 79 picture the sage doing?
o: calling in the debt, in full.
keeping the tally, and not pressing for payment.
pretending there never was a quarrel.
games.why: the chapter admits some resentment remains, and pictures the sage holding his half of the tally without demanding that the other side pay.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've drifted from, where the drift is about time, pride or awkwardness, not danger. Ask yourself two questions: is it safe, and do I want this?
If both answers are yes, find the simplest first sentence, short and true; if either is no, let them go back to the distance, and if you pray, you can bring them into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Reconciling. Two people rebuilding what was broken between them: a step past forgiveness, taken only where it's safe. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Psalm 133:1: brothers dwelling together, as one.

carryVoice: Your line: when it's safe. Where it isn't, the line is your permission to wait. Until tomorrow.
